title: The power of an imaginary coach
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton takes the hypothesis model he uses in coaching and turns it into a self-check teachers can run inside their own lessons with no coach present. He proposes an imaginary coach whose standing hypothesis is that students are not listening, do not understand, or will not remember, so that the teacher must supply evidence to refute each. Quiet, smiling, nodding classes are, he argues, poor proxies for all three. For listening he suggests Cold Call and Call and Respond; for understanding, whole-class checks such as mini-whiteboards or ABCD cards on a diagnostic question; and for memory, retrieval in later Do Nows, quizzes, homework or woven into new topics. The piece is a compact framework for replacing assumption with evidence about the gap between performance and learning.
points: The three questions of listening, understanding and remembering give teachers a simple checklist to run at regular points in any lesson.
Quiet, nodding, smiling students are poor proxies for listening, and a single correct answer or an absence of questions is a poor proxy for understanding.
Barton matches each question to a specific check: Cold Call or Call and Respond for listening, whole-class responses for understanding, and delayed retrieval for memory.
Retrieval is framed as the evidence against confusing performance in the moment with learning that lasts.
quotes: There are many poor proxies for understanding, such as one student's response, a room full of nods, or nobody asking questions. But what is the evidence that our students really understand?

Every time we give an instruction or explanation or another student speaks, the imaginary coach’s hypothesis is that our students are either not listening, do not understand, or will not remember. So, our job is to provide the critical evidence to test and - hopefully! - refute that hypothesis.

These checks for listening need to be done regularly enough, and the consequences of not listening need to be sufficiently severe, to ensure that the norm in the classroom becomes: we listen hard at all times.

Mini-whiteboards are often my go-to in a maths lesson, but using ABCD cards in response to a well-chosen multiple-choice diagnostic question can be an effective way in any subject to see who understands and who does not.
The thing to avoid here is assuming that just because students could do something at the time, they will always be able to do it. This is the distinction between performance and learning.
